bookTitle: Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (John C. Hull)
generalAssumptions: No-arbitrage principles govern pricing in liquid financial and commodity markets.
Borrowing and lending rates are equal at the continuous risk-free rate r.
Index dividend payments can be approximated as a continuous dividend yield q.
Physical storage costs and convenience yields reflect real carrying costs and operational benefits.

facts.statement: At inception t=0, the value of a forward contract f is zero and delivery price K equals F_0. At mid-life time t prior to maturity T, the value of an existing long forward contract is f = (F_t - K) * e^(-r(T-t)) = S_t - K * e^(-r(T-t)). For a short forward contract, the value is f_short = (K - F_t) * e^(-r(T-t)) = K * e^(-r(T-t)) - S_t.

variables.definition: Current market value of existing long forward contract
Current spot price of underlying asset at time t
Contract delivery price fixed at inception

facts.topic: Long Forward Contract Mid-Life Valuation Example
facts.statement: Consider a long forward contract on a non-dividend stock with delivery price K = $50 maturing in 6 months. After 3 months (remaining time tau = 0.25 years), the spot price rises to S_t = $53 and the risk-free rate is r = 6%. The value of the contract is f = 53 - 50 * e^(-0.06 * 0.25) = 53 - 49.26 = +$3.74.

numericalDetails.context: Long forward contract on non-dividend stock maturing in 6 months valued at 3 months

facts.topic: Stock Index Futures Pricing with Continuous Dividend Yield
facts.statement: A stock index is treated as an investment asset providing a continuous dividend yield q. The theoretical forward/futures price is F_0 = S_0 * e^((r - q)T), where S_0 is the spot index level, r is the risk-free rate, and q is the dividend yield.

variables.definition: Continuous dividend yield of the index portfolio

facts.statement: Index arbitrage involves simultaneous trading of stock index futures and the underlying portfolio of stocks. If F_0 > S_0 * e^((r-q)T), arbitrageurs buy the stock basket and sell futures (cash-and-carry). If F_0 < S_0 * e^((r-q)T), arbitrageurs short the stock basket and buy futures. Program trading uses computer routing systems to execute constituent trades instantly.

facts.topic: The October 1987 Crash and Index Arbitrage Breakdown (Snapshot 5.4)
facts.statement: On Black Monday (October 19, 1987), the Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 22.6%. Massive selling of S&P 500 index futures by dynamic portfolio insurance hedgers pushed futures prices to unprecedented discounts (backwardation) below cash index levels. Index arbitrage failed because NYSE's Designated Order Turnaround (DOT) system jammed with unexecuted orders, rendering cash index quotes stale and execution impossible. This led to market-wide circuit breakers and NYSE Rule 80A.

facts.topic: Currency Forwards and Covered Interest Rate Parity
facts.statement: A foreign currency is an investment asset paying a continuous dividend yield equal to the foreign risk-free rate r_f. Under covered interest rate parity, the forward exchange rate is F_0 = S_0 * e^((r - r_f)T), where S_0 is the spot exchange rate expressed as domestic currency per unit of foreign currency.

sourceCitation.section: 5.10 Forward and Futures Contracts on Currencies

variables.definition: Forward exchange rate (domestic per foreign unit)
Spot exchange rate (domestic per foreign unit)

facts.statement: Suppose spot USD/GBP is S_0 = 1.5000, US interest rate is r = 5%, and UK interest rate is r_f = 7% for T = 1 year. The theoretical forward rate is F_0 = 1.5000 * e^((0.05 - 0.07) * 1) = 1.5000 * e^(-0.02) = 1.4703. If the actual forward quote is 1.4900, an arbitrageur borrows $1,500 at 5%, converts to 1,000 GBP, deposits in the UK at 7% to yield 1,072.51 GBP, and sells GBP forward at 1.4900 to lock in $1,598.04 against a debt repayment of $1,576.91, capturing a riskless $21.13 profit per 1,000 GBP.

sourceCitation.section: 5.10 Forward and Futures Contracts on Currencies

numericalDetails.context: Covered interest arbitrage on USD/GBP with 5% US rate and 7% UK rate

facts.topic: Commodity Futures, Storage Costs and Convenience Yield
facts.statement: Commodities incur storage costs u (percentage of spot) and provide physical inventory utility known as convenience yield y. The theoretical forward price is F_0 = S_0 * e^((r + u - y)T). For investment commodities (gold/silver), y is virtually zero and F_0 = S_0 * e^((r + u)T). For consumption commodities (crude oil, copper), when spot inventory is critically scarce, y can exceed r + u, producing backwardation where forward price is lower than spot (F_0 < S_0).
